title: Jim Robinson versus Honore Dutrey as trombonists
summary: Asked whom he prefers, DeVore picks Jim Robinson for his punch, while saying Dutrey had a nice style and was gassed in World War I.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: Well, I hate to put you on the spot and you don't have to answer it. Who would you rather listen to, Jim Robinson or Henri Dutre? Jim Robinson, without a doubt. And so there's something to be said for a guy who's a real talk musician like Jim.

Yes, right. I'm not putting Jim down a bit because he had... Jim, see, it's like I say, he's learned as much music as was necessary for the band. Maybe Jim could only learn so much music, you know. Henri, on the other hand, never had the punch that Jim had. But to me, the more I listened to it, Henri had a very nice style. I'm not so sure that he didn't play quite a bit better live than he did in the records. Because I've heard Armstrong and other guys have played in that band. How many are left alive? I guess Louis is about the only one, isn't he? St. Cyril. Yeah, that's right, St. Cyril. I read an interview by him. They all like Dutre's playing. But they like Dutre's playing a lot. And he got gassed, you know, in the first world war and that he never did play as good after that.
I think one thing is that you listen to him on the Dodge records and you can hear a little better what his style was like. I think he was on a Genet Studio disadvantage.

Right, I think he has a lot to do with it too. But no matter how good he played, I think Jim played with more punch. And of course Jim to me is my favorite trombone player of all time. Because he plays the most punch of any trombone player I've heard on record or in person. And I like that the best. Like I say, Jim's a one-man rhythm section.
